The 2023 comparatives on the statement of financial position and in note 14 (Debtors) and note 17 (Creditors) are labelled 'as restated', reflecting a netting of intercompany balances under a Multilateral Netting Deed. While note 14 briefly explains the mechanics of the offset, neither that note nor any other note discloses: (a) the nature of the prior period error (i.e. whether this is a correction of a misstatement or merely a reclassification, and why the original presentation was incorrect); (b) the amount of the correction for each financial statement line affected on a gross-to-net basis with clear quantification of the restatement impact; or (c) confirmation of which other lines, if any, were affected. FRS 102 Section 10 requires that when a prior period error is corrected, the entity discloses the nature of the error and the amount of the correction for each financial statement line item affected. This disclosure is absent, meaning users cannot assess the significance or propriety of the restatement. (confidence 0.82)

The company recognises a deferred tax asset of £41,970 at 31 December 2024, of which £41,306 (approximately 98%) relates to tax losses carried forward. The company reported an operating loss in 2024 and a significant decline in profitability. While the accounting policy correctly states that recognition of deferred tax assets is limited to the extent it is probable they will be recovered against future taxable profits, the notes provide no evidence or explanation to support the recoverability of this loss-related deferred tax asset — no forward-looking profit forecasts, no discussion of the basis for concluding recovery is probable, and no disclosure of the amount of unrecognised losses (if any). Given the loss-making position and difficult trading conditions described, the absence of any recoverability assessment or disclosure is a quality concern. (confidence 0.72)

questions.question: Does this company qualify to prepare its financial statements under the micro-entity regime, or is it using the full FRS 102 framework?
questions.why: Section 1A applies only to micro-entities meeting specific turnover, balance sheet, and employee thresholds, which dramatically reduces the disclosures required.

questions.question: Is this company part of a larger group where the parent publishes consolidated accounts that already include this company's figures?
questions.why: If it is, the company may be eligible to omit certain detailed disclosures and the cash flow statement, provided it states this relief clearly in the notes.

questions.question: Is the company using an adapted balance sheet layout specifically designed for smaller entities, or the standard format?
questions.why: The adapted format simplifies presentation and allows certain line items to be combined, affecting how the balance sheet is structured and disclosed.

questions.question: Does this company have any subsidiaries, associates, or jointly controlled interests that it owns and controls?
questions.why: If it is a parent, it must consolidate or equity-account for those investments, and certain consolidation-related disclosures become mandatory.

questions.question: Is the company exempt from preparing consolidated financial statements—for instance, because its parent already does so and includes it there?
questions.why: If the company uses this exemption, it reports as a single entity only and must disclose the exemption; this avoids the need for consolidation accounting and related group disclosures.

questions.question: Is this the first year the company has prepared financial statements using FRS 102, having previously used a different accounting framework?
questions.why: First-time adopters must make specific opening adjustments and disclose transitional information about how the change affects comparative figures.

questions.question: Does the company meet the definition of a small entity—typically turnover under £10.2 million, balance sheet total under £5.1 million, and fewer than 50 employees?
questions.why: Small entities can simplify or omit several disclosures, such as related party details and segment reporting, provided they state their size status.

questions.question: During the year or in prior years, did the company acquire any subsidiaries or major business operations?
questions.why: Acquisitions require detailed disclosure of the consideration paid, identifiable assets and liabilities, any goodwill, and the impact on profit if the acquisition was mid-year.

questions.question: Did the company record any write-downs of goodwill, intangible assets, property, or other fixed assets because they fell below their book value?
questions.why: Impairments must be disclosed by class of asset, the reasons for the impairment, and how the recoverable amount was determined.

questions.question: Did the company reverse any impairment losses previously recognized on fixed assets because their value recovered?
questions.why: Reversals are allowed only in specific circumstances and must be separately disclosed with an explanation of what changed.

questions.question: Does the company hold investments in associates—companies where it has significant influence but does not control?
questions.why: Associates must be accounted for using the equity method, and their results and net assets are disclosed separately.

questions.question: Does the company operate any share schemes, such as employee share options, share awards, or matching share plans?
questions.why: Share-based payments must be measured and expensed over the vesting period, with disclosure of the scheme terms, number of instruments, and fair value methodology.

questions.question: Does the company lease any significant assets, such as property, vehicles, or equipment, where it is the user and pays rentals to a lessor?
questions.why: Leases must be classified as finance or operating; finance leases are capitalized as assets with corresponding liabilities, and both types require specific disclosures.

questions.question: Does the company own assets that it leases out to customers—for instance, property or equipment where the company retains ownership risks?
questions.why: Operating leases owned by the company are held as assets on the balance sheet, and revenue and asset details must be disclosed.

questions.question: Does the company itself prepare a consolidated group balance sheet and profit and loss account, or does it only prepare its own single-entity accounts?
questions.why: If the company prepares consolidation, it must disclose goodwill, eliminable intercompany balances, minority interests, and consolidated segment information.

questions.question: Does the company lease in any major assets such as plant, vehicles, or buildings under arrangements where the company bears the economic risks and will ultimately own them?
questions.why: Finance lease assets and the corresponding lease obligations must be capitalized and depreciated, with detailed disclosure of lease terms and future payment obligations.

questions.question: Did the company acquire another entity or merge with it using merger accounting—that is, treating it as a combination of entities under common control rather than a purchase?
questions.why: Merger accounting permits assets and liabilities to be combined at book value with no goodwill, and requires detailed disclosure of the restructuring and prior-year restatement.

questions.question: Does the company have any shared control arrangements with other parties over any entity or business operation?
questions.why: Jointly controlled entities must be accounted for using the equity method or proportionate consolidation, and their results and assets are disclosed separately.

questions.question: Does the company operate under a service concession—for instance, running a school, hospital, or infrastructure asset on behalf of a government or public authority?
questions.why: Service concessions have specialized accounting rules for recognizing the concession asset and revenue, and require detailed disclosure of the arrangement terms.

questions.question: Are these financial statements presented in a currency different from the company's day-to-day operating currency?
questions.why: When presentation currency differs from functional currency, all amounts must be retranslated, exchange gains and losses must be separately disclosed, and comparative figures must be restated.

questions.question: Is the company using an adapted profit and loss layout designed for smaller entities, or the standard multi-line format?
questions.why: The adapted format allows certain expense categories to be combined, simplifying the statement and reducing the granularity of disclosures.

questions.question: Is the company applying an adapted version of Schedule 1 profit and loss presentation rules?
questions.why: Schedule 1 adaptations allow certain smaller or qualifying entities to simplify their profit and loss presentation by combining or omitting specific line items.

questions.question: During the year, did the company change any of its accounting policies, either because of a requirement or by choice—for example, switching depreciation methods or revenue recognition approaches?
questions.why: Changes in accounting policy must be disclosed with the reasons, prior-year comparative restated figures, and the quantified impact on the current year.

questions.question: Does the company operate or contribute to a defined benefit pension scheme where it promises to pay pensions based on salary and service, rather than a defined contribution scheme?
questions.why: Defined benefit plans require actuarial valuation, recognition of the net pension obligation on the balance sheet, and detailed disclosure of assumptions and sensitivity analysis.

questions.question: Has the company issued any guarantees—such as guaranteeing a subsidiary's debt, a customer's loan, or a supplier's obligations—where the company is liable if the other party defaults?
questions.why: Financial guarantee contracts must be measured at fair value and any provision recognized, with disclosure of the nature, amount, and terms of the guarantee.

questions.question: Did the directors recommend or pay a dividend for the year?
questions.why: The directors' report must state the recommended dividend (or that none is recommended), so I need to confirm whether that statement is required.

questions.question: Did the company employ on average more than 250 people during the year?
questions.why: Above 250 employees the directors' report must include an employee-engagement statement and a disabled-persons employment policy; below that they are not required.
